name: Wolaytta
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Wolaytta (wola1242) is not in the catalog. Five sweep items reduce to three works: Downing 2004 (read; second-hand summary of Amha 1996: one H per word on penult or final), Azeb Amha 1996 (two duplicate Glottolog records; read, open access; first-hand: mora-based tone-accent, one H per simple word on the final or penultimate mora of nouns/adjectives, lexically unpredictable; verbs H on first root vowel or on the suffix; explicitly rejects the stress analysis), and Mehretu Abebe 1982 (two duplicate records; unpublished 42-page AAU BA thesis, not in AAU ETD or anywhere online; known only through Yitbarek 1983's dismissive summary; low priority). Also read on file: Yitbarek Ejigu 1983 AAU MA thesis (stress analysis: penultimate main stress in non-verbs, ultimate in verbs, predictable by word class, pp. 71-73, 77) and Wakasa 2014 (distinctive pitch, not fully predictable, p. 32). Best statement: Amha 1996 p. 114 / p. 119. If the language is added to the catalog, code it as lexical pitch-accent (final vs penultimate mora) with Amha 1996 as the deciding source, noting Yitbarek 1983 as the superseded penultimate-stress analysis. All

new_statements.quote: Thus, Wolaitta does not belong to the category of stress languages. [...] All lexical nouns and adjectives have only one high tone-accent. However, with some this high tone-accent occurs on the final vowel, while with others it occurs on the penultimate vowel. It is not possible to predict, either on the basis of word class or on the basis of meaning, whether the tone-accent will fall on the final or penultimate vowel of the noun or adjective. [p. 114] [...] Positionally, two contrasts have been observed. With very few exceptions, tone-accent is marked either on the final or the penultimate mora. [p. 119]
new_statements.citation: Azeb Amha. 1996. Tone-accent and prosodic domains in Wolaitta. Studies in African Linguistics 25(2): 111-138. doi:10.32473/sal.v25i2.107397
new_statements.locator: pp. 114 (sect. 1 end and sect. 2 opening) and 119 (sect. 2.3 summary); nouns pp. 115-116, verbs pp. 122-124
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wolaytta is a mora-counting tone-accent (pitch-accent) language, not a stress language: a simple word carries one high tone-accent, realized as an invariant H (a rise on an accented long vowel, whose second mora bears the H). In nouns and adjectives the H falls lexically on either the final or the penultimate mora; which one is not predictable from word class or meaning. Verb roots are lexically accented (H on the root's first vowel) or unaccented (H on the first vowel of the inflectional suffix / final mora of the infinitive suffix). Inflection and derivation can shift the accent or add a second H (e.g. plural of final-accented nouns, vocative -o puts H on the penult, derived nominals in -tetta/-ama/-anca have two H). In phrases the H is on the modifier, never the head.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'there is no such gradable distinction in prominence between two or more accented syllables in a word. In complex words consisting of more than one tone-accent, the accents are realized as high tone' (p. 113).
new_statements.exceptions: A few tri-/quadrisyllabic nouns ending in -nta, -etta, -puna (e.g. masunta 'wound', korima 'bull') and the numerals six to nine carry the H on the antepenultimate mora (pp. 116, ex. 5-6); object pronouns show a falling accent on a short final vowel (p. 117); ideophonic adjectives are penultimate (p. 118). Earlier analyses (Adams 1983, Yitbarek 1983) treated the system as stress, with penultimate stress in non-verbs and final stress in verbs (Yitbarek pp. 72-73, 78).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation ('absolutive') forms of nouns and adjectives, and inflected verb forms; the paper also treats phrase-level accent (H on modifiers, not heads) and morphological shifts. Wakasa 2014 (p. 33) adds that within an intonation group all but the first word lose their H, so lexical pitch contrasts surface mainly group-initially.
new_statements.identity_note: Azeb Amha 1996 describes Wolaitta = Wolaytta (wola1242) from the author's own first-language speech, no dialect named. Yitbarek 1983 and Wakasa 2014 also describe the same language (Wolaytta zone standard variety). Earlier Italian works call it Wollamo/Uallamo/Uolamo (same language).

new_statements.reading: First-hand native-speaker description: Wolaytta is a mora-based tone-accent (pitch-accent) language, not a stress language. Simple nouns and adjectives carry exactly one high tone-accent, lexically on the final or the penultimate mora (in accented long vowels the H sits on the second mora); verbs have H on the first root vowel if the root is lexically accented, otherwise on the suffix; affixation can add or shift accents. This explicitly supersedes the earlier stress analyses (Adams 1983; Yitbarek Ejigu 1983 MA, AAU, pp. 71-73: 'The main stress is on the penultimate syllable in non-verbs' and 'on the last voiced syllable on many of the verbs, but always on imperatives', predictable from word class). Wakasa 2014 (Nilo-Ethiopian Studies 19: 32) independently reports distinctive pitch whose position is 'determined for each conjugated (inflected) form of each word, and the place is not completely predictable'. Downing 2004 (pp. 107-108) only restates Amha 1996.

sources.citation: Wakasa, Motomichi. 2014. A sketch grammar of Wolaytta. Nilo-Ethiopian Studies 19: 31-44.
sources.note: p. 32-33: 'Pitch can be used distinctively. There are minimal pairs distinguished only by pitch, such as dooriis "he chose" and dooriis "he piled up"... Where the high pitch is allocated in the word is determined for each conjugated (inflected) form of each word, and the place is not completely predictable.' Words inside an intonation group lose their H except the first word; pitch not marked in the sketch. Proper nouns fall into Tone Class I (H on ending only) and II (H on stem and ending) (p. 36).

sources.quote: tone is subject to culminativity in Somali (Hyman 1981) and Wolaitta (Amha 1996). Only one High tone is allowed per word, and in compounds only the first member retains its High tone. [...] Also, tone is subject to a positional restriction, occurring generally on the penult or final syllable of the word or stem in languages like Somali, Wolaitta, and Beja (Bedawi) (Hudson1973). (However, it is not phonologically predictable where the High tone will fall, though there are morphologically predictable patterns.) [...] (3) Wolaitta pitch-accent (Amha 1996): Only one H per word, on the penult or final of word or stem
sources.note: Second-hand survey: classifies Wolaitta as a pitch-accent system (after Amha 1996) with one culminative H per word on the penult or final syllable of the word/stem, position lexically/morphologically determined rather than phonologically predictable. Adds nothing beyond Amha 1996.

sources.citation: Azeb Amha (1996). Tone-accent and prosodic domains in Wolaitta. Studies in African Linguistics 25(2): 111-138.
sources.quote: In previous studies Wolaitta has been described as a stress language (cf. Adams [1983] and Yitbarek [1983]). [...] Thus, Wolaitta does not belong to the category of stress languages. [...] All lexical nouns and adjectives have only one high tone-accent. However, with some this high tone-accent occurs on the final vowel, while with others it occurs on the penultimate vowel. It is not possible to predict, either on the basis of word class or on the basis of meaning, whether the tone-accent will fall on the final or penultimate vowel of the noun or adjective.
sources.note: First-hand (author is a native speaker). Wolaitta is a mora-counting tone-accent (pitch-accent) language, not a stress language: simple words carry one high tone-accent; in nouns and adjectives it falls lexically on either the final or the penultimate mora (p. 119: 'With very few exceptions, tone-accent is marked either on the final or the penultimate mora'); in accented long vowels the second mora bears the H. Verbs (pp. 122-124): accented roots have H on the first root vowel, unaccented roots have H on the suffix. Affixation can add or shift accents.

sources.citation: Yitbarek Ejigu. 1983. The phonology of Wolayta (generative approach). MA thesis, Addis Ababa University. 112 pp.
sources.note: Analyses it as stress, predictable from word class: sect. 2.3.1 (pp. 72-73) 'Stress is a significant factor in determining the class of words... It is predictable on the basis of morphological information. 2.3.1.2 The main stress is on the penultimate syllable in non-verbs... 2.3.1.3 The main stress is placed on the last voiced syllable on many of the verbs, but always on imperatives.' Summary p. 78: 'Stress is predictable. The main stress is on the penultimate syllable in words other than verbs, but on the ultimate syllable of voiced syllables on most of the verbs.' Superseded by Azeb Amha 1…
